name: Presbyterian Churches: Beginnings and Splits
summary: How Presbyterianism grew from Calvin's Geneva and Knox's Scottish Reformation into churches governed by elders, and how it divided in Scotland and America over revival, patronage, slavery, and theology.
place: Geneva, Scotland, England, and North America

start.label: Scottish Parliament adopts the Scots Confession, drafted by John Knox and others

end.label: ECO (A Covenant Order of Evangelical Presbyterians) forms out of the PC(USA)

key_dates.label: Westminster Assembly begins (to 1649), producing the Westminster Confession
Scottish Covenanters persecuted in the 'Killing Time'; the Wigtown martyrs drowned
First American presbytery formed at Philadelphia
Old Side–New Side split over the Great Awakening (reunited 1758)
Cumberland Presbyterian Church separates over revival and education of ministers
Disruption of the Church of Scotland
J. Gresham Machen founds what becomes the Orthodox Presbyterian Church
Northern and Southern mainline churches reunite as the PC(USA)

background.text: John Calvin organized the Geneva church under pastors, teachers, elders, and deacons; John Knox brought this model to Scotland after his exile in Geneva.

happened.text: Presbyterian churches are governed by elders in a series of courts (session, presbytery, synod, general assembly) rather than by bishops.
The Westminster Confession and Catechisms (1640s) became the doctrinal standards of most English-speaking Presbyterians.

American Presbyterians repeatedly split and reunited over revivalism (1741, 1810, 1837), slavery and the Civil War (1861), and liberal theology (1936, 1973), and more recently over ordination and sexuality.

outcomes.text: Presbyterian and Reformed churches, through the World Communion of Reformed Churches and other bodies, number tens of millions of members worldwide, with large churches in Korea, Africa, and Brazil.

condemnations.authority: General Assembly and Presbytery of New Brunswick
condemnations.reason: J. Gresham Machen suspended from the ministry, leading to the founding of the OPC (see his page)

persecution_note: Presbyterians were both persecuted and, where established, persecutors of others.

persecution.title: Persecution of the Scottish Covenanters
persecution.summary: After the Restoration, Charles II and James VII imposed bishops on the Church of Scotland. Presbyterians who held outdoor services ('conventicles') were fined, imprisoned, transported, or killed; in the 'Killing Time' of the 1680s government troops shot suspects in the field, and in 1685 two women, Margaret McLachlan and Margaret Wilson, were drowned at Wigtown for refusing an oath.

responsible.name: Scottish Privy Council and episcopal church

persecution.outcome: Ended with the Revolution of 1688–90, which restored Presbyterianism in Scotland.
